facts.text: His name is Camden Anderson, he is 4 years old, and people call him Cam.

He was diagnosed with high-risk acute lymphoblastic leukemia (a blood cancer) 3 months ago and is receiving treatment. A 4-year-old would describe it simply, e.g. his blood is sick and he takes medicine.
He had his tonsils taken out in the past (tonsillectomy).
The family's other concern noted at the visit is managing the side effects of his treatment.
His medications are vincristine and dexamethasone; a 4-year-old would just say he takes medicine and doesn't know the names.
Sometimes his tummy feels different after the medicine and food is harder to eat (parents report his appetite is different, harder to eat food).
He lives in a 2-story home with his mom and his 7-year-old brother. His bedroom is on the 2nd floor next to his brother's room.
He has a pet goldfish named Turbo.
Before his diagnosis he was very active, loved playing outside, and especially loved 'exploring' in the local parks.
Recently he has trouble keeping up with his older brother and has been staying inside watching TV. His favorite shows are Team Umizoomi and PJ Masks.
The family is managing the emotional impact of Cam's diagnosis (noted as a social/emotional concern affecting the family).
His grandmother homeschools him and his brother while his mom works full-time. He is at a preschool education level.
He has pain in various places: his bones hurt the most (7/10), his muscles ache (4/10), and his hands and feet feel tingly (2/10), rated with the Wong-Baker FACES scale.
He responds less to light touch on his hands and feet, and his feet aren't ticklish like before.
He gets tired quickly; the more intense the activity, the more it provokes his pain.
Walking is fine, but crawling and running are impaired and bring on pain. Standing up from sitting and squatting are uncomfortable (he grimaces, moves slower).
Going up and down steps is slower with some grimacing, but he can do it.

His hands are weaker: he often loses his grip on crayons when coloring, has trouble with buttons, can't pour milk for himself, though he can get a small glass of water from the fridge and catch a large ball most of the time.
He has decreased upper-body strength (attributed to dexamethasone and reduced activity); pushing or lifting things like his toy trucks is hard. Muscle tone appears decreased with some atrophy.
He gets about 30-60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity per day and does not participate in organized sports.
When he is tired he still likes drawing, playing with his 'stuffies' (stuffed animals), and watching his shows. He misses playing outside.
He eats a generally well-balanced diet with adequate fluids, about 1 sugary drink or juice per day, and no special diet - but his appetite has changed and eating is harder lately.
At his annual PT visit: heart rate 105, breathing rate 25, blood pressure 95/60, oxygen 98%. Height 3'4", weight 32 lbs, BMI 13.9.
He walked 820 feet in the 6-minute walk test. Single-leg standing: eyes open 8 seconds left / 7 seconds right; eyes closed 5 seconds left / 3 seconds right. Flexibility remains good.

He tends to favor his right side with a slight lean when sitting and standing, holds his stuffed animals with both arms across his chest with slight kyphosis, and walks with a shortened stride and uneven gait.
The family has adequate medical insurance, adequate transportation, and adequate access to healthcare providers. His primary care practitioner is Dr. Horatio Gates.

Family PAVING wellness wheel totals: Physical Activity 22, Stress 13, Attitude 21, Time-outs 23, Variety 17, Energy 20, Nutrition 14, Sleep 25, Investigations 16, Purpose 20, Social 25 (Goals total not legible in the source document).
He wants to play outside again, keep up with his brother, and go 'exploring' in the parks like before.
